title: Deadlock Avoidance: The Banker's Algorithm

sections.heading: State: Max, Allocation, Need, Available
sections.body:
The Banker's Algorithm (Dijkstra, 1965) is a *deadlock-avoidance* policy: instead of letting a system enter an unsafe state and then detecting or breaking a deadlock, it refuses any resource request that could lead there. It assumes every thread declares, in advance, the maximum number of instances of each resource type it may ever hold at once.

For $n$ threads $T_0, \ldots, T_{n-1}$ and $m$ resource types $R_0, \ldots, R_{m-1}$, the system state is four structures:

- **Max**, an $n \times m$ matrix: $Max[i][j] = k$ means $T_i$ may request at most $k$ instances of $R_j$ over its lifetime.
- **Allocation**, an $n \times m$ matrix: $Allocation[i][j] = k$ means $T_i$ currently holds $k$ instances of $R_j$.
- **Need**, an $n \times m$ matrix derived from the other two:

$$Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] - Allocation[i][j]$$

- **Available**, a length-$m$ vector: instances of each resource type not currently allocated to anyone.

Rows of Allocation and Need are treated as vectors, $Allocation_i$ and $Need_i$. Vector comparison is componentwise: $X \le Y$ iff $X[k] \le Y[k]$ for every $k$.

A state is **safe** if there is a *safe sequence* $\langle T_{i_1}, \ldots, T_{i_n}\rangle$ — an ordering of all threads such that, for every $T_{i_k}$, its remaining need can be met from Available plus whatever is held by the threads before it in the sequence:

$$Need_{i_k} \le Available + \textstyle\sum_{l<k} Allocation_{i_l}$$

If such a sequence exists, the system can run every thread to completion one at a time: finish $T_{i_1}$ first, reclaim its resources, then $T_{i_2}$ can get whatever it still needs, and so on. If no safe sequence exists the state is **unsafe** — not necessarily deadlocked, but the system can no longer *guarantee* every thread will finish. A cycle in the resource-allocation graph is a stronger, easier condition to check, but it only proves unsafety when every resource type has a single instance; with multiple instances a cycle can exist in a state that is still safe, so the graph test doesn't generalize and the Banker's Algorithm is needed instead.

sections.heading: The Safety Algorithm
sections.body:
Checking whether a state is safe is itself an algorithm, independent of any specific request. Given Available, Allocation and Need, it looks for a safe sequence directly, by simulating threads finishing in some order:

1. Initialize $Work \leftarrow Available$ and $Finish[i] \leftarrow \text{false}$ for all $i$.
2. Find an index $i$ with $Finish[i] = \text{false}$ and $Need_i \le Work$. If none exists, go to step 4.
3. Set $Work \leftarrow Work + Allocation_i$ and $Finish[i] \leftarrow \text{true}$; go to step 2.
4. The state is safe iff $Finish[i]$ is true for every $i$.

$Work$ tracks resources that would be free if every finished thread released everything it holds; each pass through step 2 asks "is there a not-yet-finished thread whose remaining need is covered by what's currently free?", and if so pretends it runs to completion and returns its resources. The order in which threads are picked *is* a safe sequence when one is found — but it need not be unique: whenever two unfinished threads both satisfy step 2 at the same point, either can go first without changing the outcome.

Each of the (at most) $n$ passes through step 2 scans up to $n$ threads and does an $O(m)$ vector comparison for each, so the whole check costs $O(m n^2)$ — the bound Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne state explicitly and set as a practice exercise to prove. It is run from scratch every time a request needs to be evaluated; nothing about a previous safety check is reusable, since Allocation and Need change with every grant.

sections.heading: The Resource-Request Algorithm
sections.body:
A request from thread $T_i$ is a vector $Request_i$. Before touching any state, the kernel runs three checks in order:

1. **Legality.** If $Request_i \not\le Need_i$, the thread has asked for more than it declared as its maximum — a programming error, not a resource shortage — and the request is refused outright.
2. **Availability.** If $Request_i \le Available$ fails, the resources simply don't exist right now; $T_i$ must block until other threads release enough.
3. **Safety.** If both checks pass, the kernel *pretends* to grant the request:

$$Available \leftarrow Available - Request_i$$

along with $Allocation_i \leftarrow Allocation_i + Request_i$ and $Need_i \leftarrow Need_i - Request_i$, and reruns the safety algorithm on this hypothetical state. If it comes back safe, the grant is made real and $T_i$ proceeds. If it comes back unsafe, the kernel rolls the three assignments back to their old values, and $T_i$ waits — even though step 2 showed the resources were physically available. This is the crux of *avoidance*: a request can be refused purely on the grounds of what it would allow other threads to eventually ask for, not because anything is currently short.

Because step 3 dominates, granting or denying a single request costs the same $O(mn^2)$ as one safety check, on top of the $O(m)$ vector comparisons in steps 1 and 2. A system that ran this on every acquisition would pay that cost on the hot path of every resource request — one reason production kernels don't run the full algorithm for general-purpose resources (see the last section).

sections.heading: Why a Safe State Guarantees No Deadlock
sections.body:
The claim behind the whole apparatus is: *safe state → no deadlock is possible, ever, regardless of how threads are scheduled from here on.* The proof is the algorithm itself, read as an induction. Suppose $\langle T_{i_1}, \ldots, T_{i_n}\rangle$ is a safe sequence for the current state. By definition $Need_{i_1} \le Available$, so if the scheduler stalls every other thread and lets $T_{i_1}$ run, $T_{i_1}$ can always eventually get whatever it still needs — it never blocks forever. When it finishes it releases $Allocation_{i_1}$, so $Available$ grows by exactly that amount. By the safe-sequence condition, that new $Available$, plus whatever $T_{i_2}$ already holds, covers $Need_{i_2}$, so $T_{i_2}$ is next in line for the same argument. Inductively, every thread in the sequence eventually finishes: there is at least one schedule with no permanent waiting, hence no deadlock.

The converse is intentionally *not* claimed. An unsafe state has no such guarantee, but "no guarantee" is not "certain failure": from an unsafe state the system may still run for a long time, one or more threads may complete normally, and a thread might release resources before asking for its maximum, restoring safety. What deadlock avoidance buys is the stronger property — a proof, checked before every grant, that no future interleaving of requests can wedge the system — at the cost of assuming every thread's maximum demand is known and fixed in advance. It sidesteps reasoning about the full space of future schedules by only needing *one* completion order to exist, not by reasoning about all of them.

sections.heading: Trade-offs and Where This Breaks Down
sections.body:
The algorithm's power comes from an assumption that is awkward in a general-purpose OS: every thread must declare $Max_i$ before it runs, and never exceed it. Kernels don't know in advance how many mutexes a thread will lock, how much heap a `malloc`-heavy program will request, or how many open file descriptors a request handler will accumulate — so there is no $Max$ matrix to check requests against. This is why the Banker's Algorithm is taught as the canonical *model* of deadlock avoidance rather than deployed as a general resource manager: Linux, for instance, uses `lockdep` to detect lock-ordering violations statically (a resource-allocation-graph-style check, not a Banker's-style admission test) and otherwise relies on deadlock *prevention* — breaking one of the four necessary conditions, e.g. a fixed global lock order — rather than avoidance.

Where the assumption does hold — every requester bounded and known ahead of time — the technique is still used in spirit: conservative two-phase locking in database concurrency control has a transaction acquire, or at least declare, its full lock set before doing any work, which is exactly a $Max_i$ commitment, and schedulability analysis for hard real-time systems similarly requires bounding a task's worst-case resource holdings before admission. Dijkstra's own motivating case was a small, fixed pool of interchangeable devices shared by batch jobs with known maximum demands — precisely the setting where declaring $Max$ up front is natural rather than a fiction.

Even within that setting, one distinction is easy to blur: the resource-allocation-graph cycle test is a valid safety check only when every resource type has a single instance. With multiple interchangeable instances of a type, a cycle can exist in the allocation graph while a safe sequence still does, so cycle detection alone would reject states that are actually fine. That is exactly why $Max$/$Allocation$/$Need$/$Available$ matrices, not a graph, are the right representation once $m > 1$.

code.caption: Safety-algorithm check run on the METU t0 snapshot (5 threads, 3 resource types); finds a safe order, not necessarily the lecturer's.

worked_example.problem:
A METU CENG334 problem set (2026 lecture slides, Week 7a, deadlocks) gives 5 processes $P_1$–$P_5$ and 3 resource types $A$ (10 instances), $B$ (5), $C$ (7), with this snapshot at $t_0$:

| | Alloc A,B,C | Max A,B,C |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0,1,0 | 7,5,3 |
| P2 | 2,0,0 | 3,2,2 |
| P3 | 3,0,2 | 9,0,2 |
| P4 | 2,1,1 | 2,2,2 |
| P5 | 0,0,2 | 4,3,3 |

a) Compute Need and Available, and show $t_0$ is safe by exhibiting a safe sequence.
b) $P_2$ requests $(1,0,2)$. Can it be granted? If so, update the state.
c) In the state after (b), $P_5$ requests $(3,3,0)$. Can it be granted?
d) In the state after (b) (independently of (c)), $P_1$ requests $(0,2,0)$. Can it be granted?
worked_example.solution:
**a) Need and safety at $t_0$.** $Need = Max - Allocation$ gives $Need_1=(7,4,3)$, $Need_2=(1,2,2)$, $Need_3=(6,0,0)$, $Need_4=(0,1,1)$, $Need_5=(4,3,1)$. Total allocated is $(7,2,5)$ against $10,5,7$ total instances, so

$$Available = (3,3,2)$$

Running the safety algorithm (scanning $P_1$ before $P_2$ before … at each pass):

| Pass | Picked | Why | Work after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P2 | $(1,2,2)\le(3,3,2)$ | $(5,3,2)$ |
| 2 | P4 | $(0,1,1)\le(5,3,2)$ | $(7,4,3)$ |
| 3 | P1 | $(7,4,3)\le(7,4,3)$ | $(7,5,3)$ |
| 4 | P3 | $(6,0,0)\le(7,5,3)$ | $(10,5,5)$ |
| 5 | P5 | $(4,3,1)\le(10,5,5)$ | $(10,5,7)$ |

$\langle P_2, P_4, P_1, P_3, P_5\rangle$ finishes everyone, so $t_0$ is safe. (This is the order the reference C program below finds by scanning lowest-index-first; the slides give a different but equally valid order, $\langle P_2, P_4, P_5, P_3, P_1\rangle$ — ties in step 2, here between $P_1$ and $P_3$ once $Work=(7,4,3)$, can be broken either way.)

**b) $P_2$ requests $(1,0,2)$.** Legality: $(1,0,2)\le Need_2=(1,2,2)$, holds. Availability: $(1,0,2)\le(3,3,2)$, holds. Tentatively grant: $Allocation_2 \to (3,0,2)$, $Need_2 \to (0,2,0)$, and

$$Available \to (2,3,0)$$

Re-running the safety algorithm on this state succeeds (e.g. $\langle P_2,P_4,P_5,P_1,P_3\rangle$), so the grant is confirmed for real.

**c) $P_5$ requests $(3,3,0)$ against $Available=(2,3,0)$.** The availability check alone fails: $3 \le 2$ is false for the $A$ component, so the request cannot be satisfied right now regardless of safety — $P_5$ waits.

**d) $P_1$ requests $(0,2,0)$ against $Available=(2,3,0)$**, independently of (c). Legality: $(0,2,0)\le Need_1=(7,4,3)$, holds. Availability: $(0,2,0)\le(2,3,0)$, holds. Tentatively grant: $Allocation_1 \to (0,3,0)$, $Need_1 \to (7,2,3)$, $Available \to (2,1,0)$. Now no thread's need fits: $Need_2=(0,2,0)\not\le(2,1,0)$ ($B$ component), $Need_4=(0,1,1)\not\le(2,1,0)$ ($C$ component), and the rest need even more $A$ than the $2$ available. The safety algorithm terminates with no thread finished, so the resulting state is **unsafe** and the request is denied — even though every unit of it was physically available. This is the same scenario Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne work through in their own text (with $T_0$–$T_4$ in place of $P_1$–$P_5$): they reach the identical conclusion, that a request for $(0,2,0)$ by the first thread "cannot be granted, even though the resources are available, since the resulting state is unsafe."

pitfalls: **Checking Request against Max instead of Need.** The legality check is $Request_i \le Need_i$, not $Request_i \le Max_i$; comparing against Max ignores what the thread already holds and lets it over-request.
**Skipping the availability check.** A request can be legal (within Need) yet still exceed Available; the algorithm must fail fast here before ever running the safety pass, as in part (c) above.
**Treating 'unsafe' as 'deadlocked'.** An unsafe state only means the algorithm can't *prove* every thread will finish — it does not mean the system is stuck now, or ever will be.

**Applying cycle detection to multi-instance resources.** The resource-allocation-graph cycle test only certifies unsafety when every resource type has exactly one instance; with multiple instances it gives false positives.

**Forgetting to roll back a rejected tentative grant.** If the hypothetical Available/Allocation/Need update turns out unsafe, all three must be restored to their pre-request values — an implementation that forgets this corrupts the real state.

**Assuming a unique safe sequence.** Ties in step 2 (two threads whose Need both fit the current Work) can be broken either way; the algorithm proves *a* safe order exists, not which one the scheduler will actually use.
applications: **Conservative two-phase locking in database concurrency control.** A transaction declares (or acquires) its entire lock set before doing any work, which is exactly a Max_i commitment, letting the manager reason about safety the same way.

**Admission control in hard real-time / safety-critical systems.** Schedulability analysis requires bounding each task's worst-case resource holdings in advance, the same assumption the Banker's Algorithm needs to run.

**Dijkstra's original motivating case: pools of interchangeable devices.** A fixed number of tape drives shared by batch jobs with declared maximum demands is the setting where a Max matrix is natural, not synthetic.

**Teaching tool for safe-vs-unsafe reasoning.** METU CENG334 uses it (including a Dining-Philosophers instance modeled as five processes competing for five single-instance chopstick resources) as the canonical worked model of deadlock avoidance, distinct from the detection and prevention approaches covered separately.
exam_focus: METU CENG334 slides (2026, Week 7a) drill the algorithm as a request-by-request trace: start from a snapshot, verify it's safe by exhibiting a safe sequence, then process a series of requests one at a time, updating Allocation/Need/Available and re-checking safety at each step.

Past midterms (334-MT1-B Q2, 334-MT1-C Q4, and the sample midterm Q4) ask students to first derive Available and Need from Allocation and Maximum, then show the safety check explicitly — graders expect the content of Available written out at each step of the trace, not just a yes/no verdict.

334-MT1-B Q2 also tests a perturbed-Available variant ("comment on safety if B has 16 instances instead of 18") and an immediate-grant question ("can this request be granted right now?"), so the safety check has to be re-run under a modified snapshot, not just memorized for the original one.

334-MT1-C's key treats a rejected request as simply canceled — the process is assumed to make a different request later rather than block indefinitely — which is the simplified bookkeeping model the grader's reference solution follows.

self_check.question: A pending request satisfies Request ≤ Need and Request ≤ Available, yet the Banker's Algorithm still refuses it. Explain how that's possible, and why the refusal doesn't mean the system is currently deadlocked.
self_check.answer: Legality and availability only check the request in isolation; the algorithm additionally requires that *granting* it leave a state from which some safe sequence still exists. It's possible for a request to be individually satisfiable but for the resulting Allocation/Need/Available to admit no safe sequence — every thread's remaining need exceeds what would be free even after any subset of the others finish. Refusing such a request keeps the system in a state with a proof that all threads can finish; it says nothing about the *current* state, which was already fine (that's why the request could be considered in the first place). Denial is a preventive measure against a state where no such proof would exist, not evidence the system is stuck now.

self_check.question: Using the $t_0$ snapshot from the worked example (P1..P5, resources A=10,B=5,C=7, Available=(3,3,2)), suppose P3 requests (2,0,0) instead of the requests discussed above. Can it be granted immediately? Show the check.
self_check.answer: Legality: Need_3 = (6,0,0), and (2,0,0) ≤ (6,0,0) holds. Availability: (2,0,0) ≤ Available=(3,3,2) holds. Tentatively grant: Allocation_3 → (5,0,2), Need_3 → (4,0,0), Available → (1,3,2). Safety algorithm on the new state: P2 fits first (Need_2=(1,2,2) ≤ (1,3,2)), giving Work=(3,3,2); then P4 fits (Need_4=(0,1,1) ≤ (3,3,2)), giving Work=(5,4,3); P3 now fits (Need_3=(4,0,0) ≤ (5,4,3)), giving Work=(10,4,5); then P5 (Need_5=(4,3,1) ≤ (10,4,5)) gives Work=(10,4,7); finally P1 (Need_1=(7,4,3) ≤ (10,4,7)) finishes everyone. The sequence ⟨P2,P4,P3,P5,P1⟩ is safe, so the request is granted immediately.

self_check.question: Why can't a general-purpose OS like Linux use the Banker's Algorithm to prevent deadlock among threads competing for mutexes, even though a mutex is a 'resource' in the same abstract sense as a tape drive?
self_check.answer: The algorithm needs a Max_i matrix — every thread's maximum future demand for every resource type, fixed before it runs — and needs to re-run an O(mn²) safety check on every acquisition. Neither holds for mutexes in a general-purpose kernel: threads create, destroy and lock mutexes dynamically as control flow dictates, so there's no way to know in advance how many a given thread will ever hold, and running a per-mutex safety pass on every lock() call would be prohibitively expensive relative to the lock operation itself. What Linux does instead is deadlock *prevention*: lockdep statically tracks the order in which locks are acquired across all execution paths and flags any cycle in that lock-ordering graph (a resource-allocation-graph-style check restricted to single-instance resources), and the convention of a fixed global lock order breaks the circular-wait condition outright rather than avoiding it dynamically per request.

key_points: Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] − Allocation[i][j]; a request must satisfy Request ≤ Need and Request ≤ Available.
A state is safe iff some thread order lets each finish using only free + already-held resources.
Safety algorithm costs O(m·n²): up to n passes, each scanning n threads with an O(m) comparison.
Unsafe ≠ deadlocked: an unsafe state just has no proof every thread finishes, not a guaranteed stall.
A request is tried tentatively, safety-checked, then rolled back if the resulting state is unsafe.
Cycle detection alone only proves unsafety when every resource type has one instance.
tagline: Grant a resource request only if the resulting state still has a safe order in which every thread can finish.
tldr: The Banker's Algorithm avoids deadlock by refusing any request that would leave the system in a state with no *safe sequence* — an order in which every thread can finish using only currently free plus already-held resources. It requires each thread to declare a maximum demand in advance, checks Request ≤ Need and Request ≤ Available, then tentatively grants and re-runs an $O(mn^2)$ safety check before committing. A safe state provably avoids deadlock by induction on the safe sequence; an unsafe state merely loses that guarantee, which is why the technique is taught as the model of avoidance even though general-purpose kernels use prevention (lock ordering) instead.
